screens.title: The Template Method Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Today we’ll learn the Template Method pattern, a simple but powerful way to keep algorithm structure fixed while letting subclasses vary specific steps. The pattern uses an abstract base class that provides a single, final template method. That template sequences calls to other methods — some concrete, some abstract, and sometimes optional hooks — and so enforces a consistent order of operations. A practical example is generating reports: every report follows the same sequence of fetch, process, format, and save, but the formatting step differs between PDF and H T M L. Using a template method keeps shared work in one place and moves the varying parts to subclasses, reducing duplication and making maintenance easier. We will study the BeverageMaker and HouseBuilder examples from the chapter, examine primitive operations and hooks, and surface common mistakes such as making the template non-final or creating too many abstract steps. By the end you should be able to design a template method safely, choose which steps are invariant, and spot where the pattern helps frameworks and ETL pipelines. Consider how this pattern separates flow control from implementation detail — why would that matter in a large codebase?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives focus your work with template methods. First, you will understand the core principle: how a base class defines an algorithm skeleton and delegates specific steps to subclasses. A concrete example is a report generator where fetch, format, and save remain ordered but formatting differs. Second, you will implement template methods in Java: define an abstract class, declare primitive operations as abstract methods, and make the template method final so subclasses cannot change the sequence. The hands-on HouseBuilder exercise in the chapter will show this in code. Third, you will analyze when the pattern is useful — frameworks, ETL pipelines, build tools — and how it improves reuse by centralizing invariant behavior. Fourth, you will identify common mistakes: creating too many abstract steps that burden subclasses, or violating the Liskov Substitution Principle by allowing subclass behavior to break expectations. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or milestone so you can verify competency by running the provided examples and spotting anti-patterns in sample code.

screens.title: What the Template Method Actually Is
screens.narratorSegment: The Template Method pattern defines an algorithm’s skeleton in an operation and defers some steps to subclasses. Concretely, an abstract base class contains a template method — often declared final — that sequences calls to other methods. Some of those calls are to concrete methods implemented by the base class for invariant behavior. Others are to abstract methods, known as primitive operations, that subclasses must implement. There are also hook methods: optional extension points that provide default behavior and may be overridden but are not required. The result is clean separation: control flow lives in the parent class, and variation lives in subclasses. A simple analogy is a cooking recipe: the recipe lists steps in order — boil, mix, bake — but the specific seasoning is left to the chef. A common misconception is that inheritance is eliminated; instead, the pattern uses inheritance intentionally to share the control flow. Another mistake is making the template method overridable; if subclasses can change the sequence, you lose the pattern’s guarantee. Consider a report pipeline where fetch and save must always occur around processing — the template enforces that contract so subclasses cannot omit those steps. How would you decide which steps are primitive and which should be concrete?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Definition
Formal definition

An abstract class defines a template method that outlines the algorithm and calls primitive operations. Subclasses implement the primitive operations; hook methods provide optional behavior with safe defaults.

Analogy
A recipe lists required steps; different cooks provide their own spices and techniques but follow the same sequence.
Misconception
Inheritance is not forbidden — it's the mechanism used to share the algorithm structure while allowing variation through primitives.
Pattern anatomy
Abstract Class
Holds the template method and some concrete methods.
Template Method
Final method that enforces step order.
Primitive Ops
Abstract methods implemented by subclasses.
Hook Methods
Optional overrides with safe defaults.
Why it matters

Centralizing control flow prevents duplicated sequence code, ensuring consistent execution order across implementations and simplifying maintenance.

screens.title: BeverageMaker Example — Code Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the BeverageMaker example from the chapter. The abstract base class defines a final prepareBeverage method that calls boilWater, brew, pourInCup, and addCondiments. Here, boilWater and pourInCup are concrete private methods representing invariant steps. Brew and addCondiments are protected abstract methods — the primitive operations — and subclasses implement them. There is also a hook customerWantsCondiments with a default true value; subclasses may override it to suppress condiments. The Coffee and Tea concrete classes implement brew and addCondiments, and can override the hook to adjust behavior. This structure preserves the order of operations while allowing differing brewing and condiment behavior. A common pitfall is making primitives public or the template non-final; both choices weaken the pattern’s guarantees. When you read the code, notice accessibility choices: private for invariant helpers, protected for primitives so subclasses can implement them, and final on the template to lock order. As you study the code block, ask yourself how you would unit test each primitive and the overall flow without relying on subclass internals. Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Code Walkthrough
Structure to observe
  • template method declared final to prevent reorder or omission of steps.
  • private concrete methods for invariant operations like boiling water.
  • protected abstract methods for primitives to let subclasses implement them.
  • hooks with default behavior to make extension optional.
Check your understanding

Can a subclass change the order of operations? No, the template is final and prevents that.

Example code (excerpt)
<!-- Abstract base: BeverageMaker -->
abstract class BeverageMaker {

  public final void prepareBeverage() {
    boilWater();
    brew();
    pourInCup();
    addCondiments(); // hook or primitive
  }

  protected abstract void brew();
  protected abstract void addCondiments();

  private void boilWater() {
    System.out.println("Boiling water");
  }

  private void pourInCup() {
    System.out.println("Pouring into cup");
  }

  protected boolean customerWantsCondiments() {
    return true; // default hook
  }
}

// Concrete Coffee and Tea implement brew and addCondiments

screens.title: Primitive Operations vs Hook Methods
screens.narratorSegment: A key design decision in a template method is choosing which steps are primitive operations and which are hooks. Primitive operations are abstract and force every subclass to implement them; use primitives when a step must be concretely defined for correct behavior, for example formatting the body of a report. Hook methods have default implementations and are optional overrides; use hooks for extension points where most subclasses won't need custom behavior, such as an optional logging step or an extra cleanup stage. If you make too many primitives, subclasses become heavy and repetitive; if you make too few, you limit flexibility. Another pitfall is exposing primitives with broad visibility: making them public can allow external callers to call steps out of sequence. Prefer protected visibility so only subclasses implement them, and keep helpers private when they are invariant. A practical test is to implement two concrete classes; if their bodies share identical code for a primitive, that step probably belongs as a concrete method in the base class instead. Finally, ask whether the subclass implementation could violate expectations — if so, reconsider whether the operation should be concrete or restricted.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Comparison
Primitive operations (must implement)
  • Declared abstract; subclasses must provide behavior.
  • Used when a step is essential and varies across implementations.
  • Visibility typically protected to restrict external calls.
Example
formatBody() for different report types.
Hook methods (optional)
  • Provide default implementation; subclasses may override.
  • Useful for optional steps like extra logging or post-processing.
  • Reduce subclass burden by supplying safe defaults.
Example
customerWantsCondiments() in BeverageMaker.
Common mistake
Making too many abstract methods forces repetitive implementations; prefer concrete defaults when behavior is shared.

screens.title: Template Method Structure — Typical Step Sequence
screens.narratorSegment: A canonical template method sequences steps where some are invariant and others vary. A common sequence is: prepare resources, fetch data, process data, format output, finalize and save. In the abstract class, implement preparation and finalization as concrete methods to ensure they always run. Place fetch, process, and format as primitive operations if they must differ across subclasses. Include hooks between steps when you expect optional behavior, for instance an optional validation hook after processing. Always make the template method final so subclasses cannot skip or reorder steps. For resource-sensitive steps, include concrete cleanup code or a finalizing hook that guarantees resource release even if a primitive throws an exception. A misconception to avoid is assuming hooks are always empty; they should provide safe defaults that preserve invariants. When converting an existing pipeline to this pattern, extract the invariant sequence into a template and progressively pull variant code into abstract primitives until each subclass only contains what truly varies. In practical terms, a canonical sequence and how to enforce it safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: When to Use the Template Method Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The Template Method is especially useful when many classes share a common high-level flow but differ in specific steps. Frameworks often define control flow and let user code override primitive operations; the chapter cites servlet frameworks where the container calls doGet and doPost as hooks within a larger request lifecycle. ETL pipelines are another natural fit: extract, transform, and load are fixed phases while extraction and transformation vary by source. Build processes and report generators are similar: you want a central structure for correctness and logging, and variation points for source or format differences. However, if variation requires changing the order of steps frequently, the pattern is a poor fit — prefer composition or strategy in those cases. Another practical consideration is testability: template methods make it straightforward to write tests that assert sequence execution, while primitives are individually testable via concrete subclasses or test doubles. Finally, use the pattern when you can clearly separate invariants from variants; if such separation is fuzzy, refactor smaller pieces before applying the pattern. When to Use the Template Method Pattern means apply the pattern when a stable sequence must be preserved and individual steps differ by implementation or data source.. In practical terms, frameworks, pipelines, and repeated sequences with variation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Frameworks
Frameworks define the flow and call developer-provided implementation points; this enforces a contract between framework and app code.
ETL Pipelines

screens.title: Safety Notes: LSP, Final methods, and Resource Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Designing template methods requires care to avoid subtle bugs. First, respect the Liskov Substitution Principle: any subclass implementation of a primitive operation must preserve the expectations of the base class. If a subclass changes semantics in a way that breaks callers of the base type, you have violated LSP. Second, mark the template method final so subclasses cannot alter the algorithm sequence; otherwise the pattern's guarantees disappear. Third, when primitives perform input and output or access shared state, the template should either manage error handling and cleanup or provide hooks specifically designed for cleanup; this centralizes resource management and reduces duplication. In multithreaded contexts, protect shared state accessed by the template or primitives with appropriate synchronization. Finally, prefer sensible default implementations for hook methods so subclasses that don’t need to customize behavior remain lightweight. A common misconception is that the template must make everything abstract — it should only require what truly varies while keeping the rest centralized for correctness and reuse. Safety Notes: LSP, Final methods, and Resource Handling means keep the template final, ensure primitives preserve contracts, centralize cleanup, and provide safe defaults for hooks.. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes weaken the Template Method pattern. First, making the template method non-final allows subclasses to change the order of steps, which undermines the algorithm contract. Second, declaring too many abstract methods forces subclasses to implement trivial or shared behavior, leading to duplication and maintenance pain. Third, violating the Liskov Substitution Principle happens when a subclass implements a primitive with behavior that changes expected results or side effects; that leads to surprising behavior when clients use the base type. Fourth, exposing primitive methods publicly lets external code call steps out of order. Fifth, neglecting resource cleanup in the template and scattering it across subclasses increases the risk of leaks. To avoid these, keep the template final, choose a minimal set of primitives, prefer protected visibility, and centralize cleanup or supply a cleanup hook. When in doubt, implement a default concrete behavior and extract to abstract only when a real, tested need for variation emerges. fullNarratorScript:
Today we’ll learn the Template Method pattern, a simple but powerful way to keep algorithm structure fixed while letting subclasses vary specific steps. The pattern uses an abstract base class that provides a single, final template method. That template sequences calls to other methods — some concrete, some abstract, and sometimes optional hooks — and so enforces a consistent order of operations. A practical example is generating reports: every report follows the same sequence of fetch, process, format, and save, but the formatting step differs between PDF and H T M L. Using a template method keeps shared work in one place and moves the varying parts to subclasses, reducing duplication and making maintenance easier. We will study the BeverageMaker and HouseBuilder examples from the chapter, examine primitive operations and hooks, and surface common mistakes such as making the template non-final or creating too many abstract steps. By the end you should be able to design a template method safely, choose which steps are invariant, and spot where the pattern helps frameworks and ETL pipelines. Consider how this pattern separates flow control from implementation detail — why would that matter in a large codebase?

These four objectives focus your work with template methods. First, you will understand the core principle: how a base class defines an algorithm skeleton and delegates specific steps to subclasses. A concrete example is a report generator where fetch, format, and save remain ordered but formatting differs. Second, you will implement template methods in Java: define an abstract class, declare primitive operations as abstract methods, and make the template method final so subclasses cannot change the sequence. The hands-on HouseBuilder exercise in the chapter will show this in code. Third, you will analyze when the pattern is useful — frameworks, ETL pipelines, build tools — and how it improves reuse by centralizing invariant behavior. Fourth, you will identify common mistakes: creating too many abstract steps that burden subclasses, or violating the Liskov Substitution Principle by allowing subclass behavior to break expectations. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or milestone so you can verify competency by running the provided examples and spotting anti-patterns in sample code.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical skills and analysis. You will implement the pattern by writing an abstract class that exposes primitive operations as abstract methods while keeping shared steps concrete. The chapter’s BeverageMaker and AbstractHouseBuilder examples show how to place common work such as boiling water or laying a foundation in the base class. Next, you will analyze design trade-offs: decide which steps must be invariant and which should be hooks or abstract. For example, a hook method with a safe default prevents forcing all subclasses to implement optional behavior. Finally, you will inspect anti-patterns: too many abstract methods create a heavy burden on subclasses, and allowing the template to be overridden can break invariants and violate the Liskov Substitution Principle. Each objective includes a milestone you can verify by running examples and checking that different concrete classes substitute cleanly without changing the algorithm flow.

The Template Method pattern defines an algorithm’s skeleton in an operation and defers some steps to subclasses. Concretely, an abstract base class contains a template method — often declared final — that sequences calls to other methods. Some of those calls are to concrete methods implemented by the base class for invariant behavior. Others are to abstract methods, known as primitive operations, that subclasses must implement. There are also hook methods: optional extension points that provide default behavior and may be overridden but are not required. The result is clean separation: control flow lives in the parent class, and variation lives in subclasses. A simple analogy is a cooking recipe: the recipe lists steps in order — boil, mix, bake — but the specific seasoning is left to the chef. A common misconception is that inheritance is eliminated; instead, the pattern uses inheritance intentionally to share the control flow. Another mistake is making the template method overridable; if subclasses can change the sequence, you lose the pattern’s guarantee. Consider a report pipeline where fetch and save must always occur around processing — the template enforces that contract so subclasses cannot omit those steps. How would you decide which steps are primitive and which should be concrete?

Let's walk through the BeverageMaker example from the chapter. The abstract base class defines a final prepareBeverage method that calls boilWater, brew, pourInCup, and addCondiments. Here, boilWater and pourInCup are concrete private methods representing invariant steps. Brew and addCondiments are protected abstract methods — the primitive operations — and subclasses implement them. There is also a hook customerWantsCondiments with a default true value; subclasses may override it to suppress condiments. The Coffee and Tea concrete classes implement brew and addCondiments, and can override the hook to adjust behavior. This structure preserves the order of operations while allowing differing brewing and condiment behavior. A common pitfall is making primitives public or the template non-final; both choices weaken the pattern’s guarantees. When you read the code, notice accessibility choices: private for invariant helpers, protected for primitives so subclasses can implement them, and final on the template to lock order. As you study the code block, ask yourself how you would unit test each primitive and the overall flow without relying on subclass internals. A key design decision in a template method is choosing which steps are primitive operations and which are hooks. Primitive operations are abstract and force every subclass to implement them; use primitives when a step must be concretely defined for correct behavior, for example formatting the body of a report. Hook methods have default implementations and are optional overrides; use hooks for extension points where most subclasses won't need custom behavior, such as an optional logging step or an extra cleanup stage. If you make too many primitives, subclasses become heavy and repetitive; if you make too few, you limit flexibility. Another pitfall is exposing primitives with broad visibility: making them public can allow external callers to call steps out of sequence. Prefer protected visibility so only subclasses implement them, and keep helpers private when they are invariant. A practical test is to implement two concrete classes; if their bodies share identical code for a primitive, that step probably belongs as a concrete method in the base class instead. Finally, ask whether the subclass implementation could violate expectations — if so, reconsider whether the operation should be concrete or restricted.

A canonical template method sequences steps where some are invariant and others vary. A common sequence is: prepare resources, fetch data, process data, format output, finalize and save. In the abstract class, implement preparation and finalization as concrete methods to ensure they always run.
